extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties litigating before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules governing protective orders, designation, filing, handling, modification, and limitations on discovery (including depositions) in TTAB proceedings. Covers the Board's standard protective order, stipulations, redaction and ESTTA procedures, and post-termination handling of confidential materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment and sanctions for access to protected information
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who are not a party or attorney must sign an acknowledgement form agreeing to be bound by the standard protective order during and after the proceedings as a condition for obtaining access to protected information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has the authority to sanction attorneys and individuals determined to be in breach during a proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to confidential information is not automatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to a party’s confidential, highly confidential or trade secret/commercially sensitive information is not provided as a matter of course, but rather must only be provided in response to a proper and relevant discovery request or when the party chooses to use such information in support of its case at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must actively utilize the provisions when seeking to designate protected information; the burden falls on the party seeking to designate information as protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to designate waives confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to designate a discovery response or submission as confidential under the terms of the protective order and/or redact confidential portions thereof, the confidentiality of the information is deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing or responding, the designating party has a duty to make a meaningful effort to designate only that information that warrants the designated level of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to avoid overdesignation; reasonableness of designations
rubrics_metrics.description: The party seeking to designate information as confidential, highly confidential or trade secret has a duty to make a meaningful effort to designate only that information that warrants the designated level of protection; excessive markings often indicate improper designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (e.g., General Mills, Blackhorse, Georgia Pacific) show overdesignation complicates the record and may lead to redesignation or show-cause orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality does not excuse withholding properly discoverable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties cannot withhold properly discoverable information on the basis of confidentiality since the terms of the Board’s standard protective order automatically apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party has refused to provide discoverable information on such grounds, the Board may order the party to provide such information consistent with the terms of the protective order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may modify Board's standard protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are free to modify the terms of the Board’s standard protective order, and are encouraged to discuss any proposed modifications during their discovery conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modifications upon stipulation or motion, parties should file a copy of the executed agreement with the Board; see TBMP § 412.02(a) for further information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification upon stipulation — filing and binding effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If the parties choose to modify the terms of the Board’s standard protective order and enter into their own stipulated protective order, a copy of the executed agreement should be filed with the Board. The terms of the agreement are binding as of the date the agreement is signed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a stipulated order may not be used to circumvent 37 CFR § 2.27(d) and (e) regarding public inspection of files, and parties should not wait for Board acknowledgement to act in accordance with the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro se litigants and in-house counsel access restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Board’s standard protective order, pro se litigants and in-house counsel do not have access to trade secret/commercially sensitive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial burden of retaining counsel is not good cause to amend the order; in-house counsel seeking access must show they are not involved in the employer-litigant's competitive decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: In camera inspection when relevance/confidentiality disputed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Board cannot determine from the parties' arguments whether a document is relevant and/or confidential, the Board may request a copy of the document for in camera inspection, after which the document will be returned to the party who submitted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amazon Technologies v. Wax (in camera inspection supported designation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — definition of confidential/trade secret material
rubrics_metrics.description: A modified protective order typically may include a provision clarifying the definition of the type of material to be considered confidential or trade secret information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should explicitly state what categories of material are covered to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — description of how confidential information is handled
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders should describe the manner in which confidential or trade secret information is to be handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can include labeling, storage, transmission, access controls, and procedures for filing and redaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — requirement to designate prior to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A protective order may require that a party claiming confidentiality or trade secret protection designate the information covered by the claim prior to disclosure of the information to the discovering party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance designation helps the discovering party and the Board identify and treat sensitive materials appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — reasonable basis for designation
rubrics_metrics.description: The protective order may provide that a party may not designate information as confidential or trade secret unless the party has a reasonable basis for believing that the information is, in fact, confidential or trade secret in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfounded or blanket confidentiality claims may be challenged and redesignated by the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — exclusions to confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders typically provide that designated confidential/trade secret information may not include information which (a) at or prior to disclosure is known to or independently developed by the discovering party; (b) is public knowledge or becomes available to the public without violation; (c) is revealed to the public by a person having the unrestricted right to do so; or (d) is acquired by the discovering party from a third party lawfully possessing the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions narrow the scope of protectable material and prevent misuse of confidentiality claims to cover public or previously-known information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — specification of persons who may access
rubrics_metrics.description: The protective order should specify the persons to whom confidential or trade secret information may be disclosed (e.g., outside counsel; in-house counsel; counsel's necessary legal and clerical personnel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties often list categories of individuals and may restrict access for pro se or other categories as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — advising recipients of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons to whom confidential or trade secret information is disclosed shall be advised of the existence and terms of the protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically recipients must sign an acknowledgement and be informed they are bound by the order's terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — limitation on use of protected information
rubrics_metrics.description: The protective order should provide that the discovering party will not disclose or make use of confidential or trade secret information provided to it under the order except for purposes of the proceeding in which the information is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits disclosure and use outside the litigation and is central to the protective order's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order content — dispute-resolution mechanisms for designations
rubrics_metrics.description: The order should specify the means for resolving disputes over whether particular matter constitutes confidential or trade secret information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms can include meet-and-confer, motions to the Board, and in camera submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing confidential materials — electronic designation and dual-version requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for material designated as confidential or trade secret to be made of record, it shall be submitted to the Board electronically designated as 'CONFIDENTIAL' in ESTTA or by paper in a separate sealed envelope; for confidential or trade secret submissions filed either via ESTTA or by paper, two versions are required – a confidential version as well as a redacted version available for public viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic filing using ESTTA is preferred; if filing via ESTTA select 'CONFIDENTIAL Opposition, Cancellation or Concurrent Use'. Confidential submissions will not be publicly viewable though docket entries are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redaction rule of reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party or attorney must file protected information with the Board, the protected information or portion of the brief discussing the same should be redacted from the remainder. A rule of reasonableness should dictate how redaction is effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a sentence or short paragraph is confidential, cover that portion; if most of a page is confidential, file the page under seal. Filing an entire submission under seal should be very rare. Failure to provide a redacted version may lead to waiver of confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper filing procedures and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper submissions of material designated as confidential should be filed in a separate sealed envelope or other sealed container prominently marked with the word 'CONFIDENTIAL' and bearing information identifying the proceeding and the nature of the contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorneys often attach a statement such as 'FILED UNDER SEAL SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER.' Envelopes should identify the proceeding number and describe contents (e.g., 'Applicant's Answers to Opposer's Interrogatories 8 and 19').

rubrics_metrics.name: Return or destruction of confidential materials after termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 30 days after the final termination of this proceeding, the parties and their attorneys shall return to each disclosing party the protected information disclosed during the proceeding, including any briefs, memoranda, summaries, and the like, or alternatively the disclosing party may request destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proceeding is terminated only after final order and resolution or lapse of appeal; the Board's jurisdiction over parties ends at termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to stipulate protective order for post-termination enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is advisable for both the parties and their attorneys to sign a stipulated protective order so that it is clear they are all bound thereby and that they have created a contract which may survive the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty exists whether the Board can order parties to enter into a contract governing protection after the proceeding; enforceability outside the Board is for a court to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's handling of confidential materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential materials submitted in paper form filed under seal are stored by the Board in a secure location and are disclosed only to the Board and to those people specified in the protective order as having the right to access; confidential material will not be disclosed in orders or decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After final determination, the Board will contact parties to arrange return or retrieval or require consent to disposal; unclaimed materials may be destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to issue other protective orders under 37 CFR § 2.120(f) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: On motion pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(f), showing good cause, the Board may make any order which justice requires to protect a party from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue burden or expense, including orders described in clauses (A) through (H) of Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of orders include forbidding disclosure, specifying terms/time/place, prescribing discovery methods, limiting scope, designating persons present, sealing depositions, protecting trade secrets, and sealed simultaneous filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause standard for protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish good cause, the movant must submit 'a particular and specific demonstration of fact, as distinguished from stereotyped and conclusory statements.' The moving party seeking a protective order bears the burden of showing good cause and must demonstrate that its ability to litigate will be prejudiced, not merely increase the difficulty of managing the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cause is a factual determination weighing the nature and character of the information sought against the factual issues in the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion upon grant or denial of motion for protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board grants a motion for a protective order it may direct the parties to prepare an order with mutually agreeable terms, may approve a proffered protective order, may order adherence to the Board’s standard protective order, or provide whatever relief the Board deems appropriate. If denied in whole or part, the Board may order discovery on just conditions (other than awarding expenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should confer in good faith before seeking Board intervention; see cited cases for examples of relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders limiting or prohibiting depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although issuance of a protective order totally prohibiting a deposition occurs only in extraordinary circumstances, the Board has discretion to limit a deposition or order that a discovery deposition not be had if the discovery sought is obtainable from other sources that are more convenient and less burdensome or duplicative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movant bears the burden to show good cause with particular and specific facts. Lack of personal knowledge is generally insufficient; the Board may grant protection for high-level executives if there are other persons with equal or greater knowledge. If movant meets initial burden, burden shifts to proponent of deposition to show unique or superior knowledge. Alternatives include depositions of lower-level employees, Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) depositions, requests for admissions, interrogatories, or requests for production. Medical or health-based requests require a specific and documented factual showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations tied to discovery period, deposition count, and duplicate depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may file a motion for protective order if a notice of deposition would exceed the permitted number of ten discovery depositions, result in a second deposition of an individual, or result in a deposition being taken outside the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assertion that the deponent is too busy or that the examination would cause undue labor, expense, or delay is generally insufficient by itself.
